question: In December 2019, in Addis Ababa, during her first overseas visit after taking office, the President of the Commission Ms von der Leyen honoured President Abiy Ahmed with gifts in the form of assistance amounting to at least EUR 150 million.

After instigating three civil wars, the cost of which (including what has been destroyed) runs to EUR 48 billion, he is now intending to build the planet’s biggest palace complex across 500 ha, in his capital city, at a cost of EUR 10-15 billion. For the period 2021/2027, the Commission earmarked EUR 1 billion in development assistance for Ethiopia, confirming that with a EUR 650 million tranche in October 2020.

Could the Commission explain to what extent the next civil war or the President’s megalomania will be financed by this money – European taxpayers’ money – either directly or by replacing and redeploying funds within the Ethiopian Government budget?
answer: During the war in northern Ethiopia, the EU suspended financial assistance to the government to avoid risks of supporting an economy of war and postponed the launch of the multiannual indicative programme (MIP) for the country.

The EU provided funds exclusively for the direct support to the population, via individual measures (EUR 339 million from the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument — Global Europe (NDICI-GE)), and for humanitarian life-saving assistance to the most vulnerable, via EU’s humanitarian partners (EUR 350 million between 2020 and 2024).

As per the European Council Conclusion of 24 April 2023 (1), the EU supports the agreement for lasting peace through a permanent cessation of hostilities concluded in November 2022. This underpinned the approval of EU’s cooperation framework with Ethiopia (MIP 2024-2027 — EUR 650 million). This provides basis for a gradual re-engagement with Ethiopia (2).

However, further normalisation of EU’s relations with Ethiopia will be based on progress on transitional justice including accountability for human rights violations during the war. The launch of the MIP foresees an active political and policy dialogue. Thus, it ensures a purpose-bound traceable financing and protects the EU funding from being diverted for unintended purposes.
As such, the EU funding will be used as a leverage towards the peace process, economic reforms and support to the population.
